title: Jackie Jormp Jomp

jokes.text: It's pronounced 'weener-slave.'
jokes.setup: A character named 'Winerslav' corrects the pronunciation of his own name at a sexual harassment seminar.
jokes.punchline: The 'correct' pronunciation is 'weener-slave,' which is even more inappropriate than the mispronunciation — at a sexual harassment seminar.
jokes.explanation: A brilliantly layered joke: the setting (sexual harassment seminar) makes the punchline land twice as hard. The joke earns its subversion because the correction makes things worse, not better. Extremely economical — three words do all the work. High rewatch value because the setup is so perfectly constructed.

jokes.text: The seminar facilitator declares his own mildly awkward joke about someone eager to return to work 'a very appropriate and very, very funny joke.'
jokes.setup: The facilitator makes a tepid observation about Liz being eager to get back to work.
jokes.punchline: He immediately labels it 'a very appropriate and very, very funny joke,' which is the actual joke — the self-congratulation for a non-joke at a harassment seminar.
jokes.explanation: Works as a meta-commentary on the kind of performatively safe humor that HR seminars produce. The self-labeling of a bad joke as funny is a reliable comic device, and the framing within a sexual harassment seminar gives it added texture. Competent but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Jenna: 'Jack, I did not hit that Asian page. I was just swinging my arm and she walked into me. Twice.'
jokes.setup: Jenna defensively insists she did not commit assault on a page.
jokes.punchline: 'Twice.' — the single word escalation that confirms she absolutely did it.
jokes.explanation: The one-word punchline 'Twice.' is perfectly timed and delivered. The joke is deeply character-specific — only Jenna's oblivious narcissism could produce this logic. The rhythm of the denial followed by self-incriminating elaboration is a classic structure executed with great economy. Approaches the 8-anchor quality.

jokes.text: Wait. We can call her Janis Joplin? We got the life rights? It's not Janie Jimplin anymore?
jokes.setup: Jack mentions a Janis Joplin biopic.
jokes.punchline: Jenna reveals the placeholder name they were using was 'Janie Jimplin,' suggesting they'd already gotten far into production with an almost-identical name.
jokes.explanation: Good absurdist setup — 'Janie Jimplin' is close enough to the real name to be hilariously useless as a legal workaround, which is the joke. It establishes the running gag of the film's legal/naming problems.

jokes.text: Apparently, neither name cleared. It looks like your character's going to be called Jackie Jormp-Jomp.
jokes.setup: Jenna assumes the life rights have been cleared for Janis Joplin.
jokes.punchline: Neither name was cleared, and the new name — Jackie Jormp-Jomp — is so phonetically absurd it becomes the episode's title and running gag.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's tent-pole jokes. 'Jackie Jormp-Jomp' is an inspired piece of comedy writing — it's the perfect legally-distinct-but-obviously-Janis-Joplin name. The cadence is funny, the absurdity of getting FURTHER from the real name is funny, and it becomes a running gag that pays off throughout. High quotability.

jokes.text: Jenna: 'Oh, okay. So what's the good news?' Jack: 'I didn't say there was any.'
jokes.setup: Jack delivers a series of bad news about the biopic.
jokes.punchline: Jenna assumes there must be good news coming; Jack flatly corrects her.
jokes.explanation: A clean, well-delivered beat that showcases both characters. Jenna's optimism in the face of clear disaster is a reliable character note, and Jack's clipped correction is perfectly in voice. The joke type is common but executed competently.

jokes.text: You're holding that upside down.
jokes.setup: Jenna is looking at a score sheet, apparently pleased to see '100.'
jokes.punchline: Jack notes she's holding it upside down — the score was actually 001, i.e., essentially zero.
jokes.explanation: A clean visual-to-dialogue joke. The misdirection (100 vs. 001) is well-structured and Jack's flat delivery without explanation is ideal. Good economy.

jokes.text: Jenna sings a fragment: 'someday there will be a black president' as her Woodstock performance.
jokes.setup: Jenna describes her duet with 'Jimi Hendrickson' at 'Woodstocks.'
jokes.punchline: The lyric she sings is a completely anachronistic, non-Janis-Joplin non sequitur — 'someday there will be a black president' — as if that was a real period song.
jokes.explanation: A sharp absurdist gag that mocks both the creative bankruptcy of the biopic and Jenna's delusion. The Obama-era topicality adds a layer. The joke is in the specific invented lyric, which is very 30 Rock — it rewards attention.

jokes.text: Jenna: 'Do you need a sex tape released? 'Cause I got a wrdne. It's night vision and you can see that his buddy is robbing me.'
jokes.setup: Jack says he needs Jenna's help with PR.
jokes.punchline: Jenna immediately offers a pre-existing sex tape — but it's a crime scene, not a glamour move; someone is actively robbing her during the filming.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The offer of a sex tape is expected given the PR context, but the punchline subverts it completely — the tape documents a robbery, not a fame play. The detail that 'his buddy is robbing me' is layered and specific. Only Jenna's bizarre, victimized, opportunistic life could produce this. Highly quotable, excellent character integration. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: I'll set aside my feud with Raven-Symoné for one day. But she knows what she did.
jokes.setup: Jack tells Jenna to attend the Kids' Choice Awards to promote the film.
jokes.punchline: Jenna reveals she has an ongoing feud with Raven-Symoné, grudgingly agrees to a truce, but adds the ominous caveat 'But she knows what she did.'
jokes.explanation: A classic 30 Rock background-detail joke. The specificity of Raven-Symoné as the target, combined with the completely unexplained but utterly committed 'she knows what she did,' is a masterclass in comedy economy. The audience's imagination fills in something funnier than anything the writers could specify.

jokes.text: Jenna: 'I'll set aside my feud with Raven Simone for one day. But she knows what she did.'
jokes.setup: Jack tells Jenna to attend the Kids' Choice Awards for PR.
jokes.punchline: Jenna has a feud with Raven-Symoné — and the dangling 'but she knows what she did' is left completely unexplained.
jokes.explanation: The unexplained grievance is a perfect comedic move — the joke is stronger for withholding the reason. 'But she knows what she did' has become genuinely quotable shorthand. Excellent economy and strong character integration (only Jenna would have a feud with a children's entertainer and treat it as reasonable).

jokes.text: Kenneth yells 'Mr. Donaghy, help! Rule breaking!' when Liz tries to take a script.
jokes.setup: Liz, on suspension, tries to grab a script from Kenneth.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth immediately calls for adult intervention as if a capital crime is occurring, shrieking 'Rule breaking!' with genuine horror.
jokes.explanation: A strong Kenneth character beat — his absolute fealty to rules and authority is a defining trait, and 'Rule breaking!' has the breathless panic of a genuine Kenneth emergency. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Jack: 'Remember that time I came back from the world economic forum with mono and missed a week of work and I wanted to pull my hair out but I couldn't because it's too thick?'
jokes.setup: Jack is empathizing with Liz about missing work.
jokes.punchline: The relatable anecdote pivots to a hyper-specific Jack detail — catching mono at Davos, and his hair being too thick to pull out in frustration.
jokes.explanation: Quintessential Jack Donaghy — the attempt at relatable empathy is immediately undercut by elite specifics (world economic forum, too-thick hair). The hair detail is the kind of vain, oblivious self-congratulation that makes Jack distinctive. Very strong character integration.

jokes.text: Jack says 'you start bouncing off the walls, spend your days jabbering at doormen' — Liz fires back, 'Hey, I brighten their day.'
jokes.setup: Jack warns that work-addicted people go stir-crazy without the office.
jokes.punchline: Liz's defensive non-denial confirms she's already been jabbering at doormen — and her self-assessment is that she's doing them a favor.
jokes.explanation: A quick, efficient joke that reveals Liz's lack of self-awareness. The rhythm of Jack's description → Liz's implicit confirmation → her defensive spin is tight and character-accurate. Good economy.

jokes.text: Frank's hat says 'constant cving.' — Liz: 'He could do better.'
jokes.setup: One of Liz's final requests before leaving is to find out what Frank's hat says.
jokes.punchline: 'Constant cving' is nonsensical enough to be funny as a running gag payoff, and Liz's critical evaluation ('He could do better') is its own joke about her priorities.
jokes.explanation: Frank's rotating hats are a long-running visual gag. The chosen phrase is arbitrary enough to be funny, and Liz judging it critically is a nice character touch. Competent running gag maintenance.

jokes.text: Lutz/writer: 'The whole thing is loosely based on an evening I spent with Isaiah Thomas.'
jokes.setup: Writers are discussing how strict the sexual harassment materials are.
jokes.punchline: One writer casually reveals he had a lawless evening with actual NBA figure Isaiah Thomas — implying he was the perpetrator or victim of real harassment.
jokes.explanation: Works because Isaiah Thomas had real-life sexual harassment controversy, making this a topical dark joke. The casual delivery ('loosely based on') is funny in itself. Good economy — a dense joke in a few words.

jokes.text: Kenneth: 'Ms. Vieira made me throw it away. And said pretty boys like me shouldn't be filling their heads with ideas.'
jokes.setup: The writers ask if Kenneth has read the sexual harassment policy.
jokes.punchline: A Today Show anchor (implied to be Meredith Vieira) made Kenneth throw away his rights document and told him pretty boys shouldn't have ideas — confirming Kenneth is being harassed.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely great joke. The inversion of the standard harassment dynamic (powerful female celebrity harassing innocent male Kenneth) is original, the celebrity name-drop has a specific twist (not just a mention), and Kenneth's obliviousness to being victimized is perfect character work. 'Pretty boys like me shouldn't be filling their heads with ideas' is the kind of line that earns its own laugh separately from the premise. Justifiably scores near the 8-anchor.

jokes.text: Hi, Frank. / Hello. / Coworker.
jokes.setup: Frank and a coworker, now aware of harassment rules about in-office relationships, greet each other after reading the handbook.
jokes.punchline: The greeting degrades to Frank saying just 'Coworker' — the most legally sanitized possible human interaction.
jokes.explanation: Excellent economy — one word ('Coworker') is the entire joke. The awkwardness of replacing a name with a job descriptor after reading the harassment pamphlet is a perfect escalation of corporate paranoia. Very punchy.

jokes.text: Liz, talking to her building's doorman: 'My job is very stressful. But in the end, I get paid to make people laugh. We have a saying that laughter is the best medicine, so I'm kind of like a doctor here.'
jokes.setup: Liz is jabbering at the doorman, showing Jack was right about her behavior.
jokes.punchline: Liz has convinced herself she's 'kind of like a doctor' because she works on a comedy show — peak self-aggrandizing delusion while she's literally banished from her job.
jokes.explanation: The payoff to Jack's prediction is satisfying. Liz's grandiose self-assessment ('kind of like a doctor') is a good character beat, but the joke is a bit long and loses steam compared to the callback setup. Functional.

jokes.text: 'Not even the time I had that virus they kept saying only raccoons get.'
jokes.setup: Liz is reflecting on her dedication to work, saying she's never missed a show.
jokes.punchline: The specific exemption — a raccoon disease — is absurd and specific enough to be very funny.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully specific piece of 30 Rock absurdism. The detail that doctors 'kept saying' only raccoons get it implies Liz contracted it more than once, or at minimum that it required explanation. The phrase is extremely quotable and has the precision that distinguishes great absurdist comedy from random-equals-funny. Very high economy.

jokes.text: Liz has been living in her building for four years and has never noticed the gym or the vending machines.
jokes.setup: Liz bumps into neighbor Emily going to the building gym.
jokes.punchline: Liz has lived there four years and didn't know a gym or vending machines existed — confirming she's never been home long enough to explore.
jokes.explanation: A solid character-defining moment — Liz's workaholism manifesting as total ignorance of her own building. The vending machine follow-up question is a nice additional beat showing her priorities. Functional and character-consistent.

jokes.text: No, I'm Liz. I've lived here for four years.
jokes.setup: Emily asks Liz if she's new to the building.
jokes.punchline: Liz has lived there four years and never noticed the gym or vending machines — implying she's been working so hard she's essentially a stranger in her own home.
jokes.explanation: A relatable observational joke about workaholic culture. The specificity of 'four years' makes it land better than a vaguer timeframe would. Solid but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Liz: 'Right now I should be standing in a toilet stall so nobody bothers me while I eat lunch. God, I miss it.'
jokes.setup: Emily gently suggests Liz seems lost without her job.
jokes.punchline: Liz's vision of workplace bliss is hiding in a toilet to eat alone — and she's genuinely nostalgic for it.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and a genuinely great Liz Lemon character moment. The specific detail (toilet stall, eating lunch, specifically to avoid people) is perfectly observed and executed. 'God, I miss it.' is the ideal kicker — the pathos is funny because she's genuinely nostalgic for a pathetic situation. Highly quotable and ranks among the episode's top moments.

jokes.text: Liz immediately identifies that Emily's candy drawer would need a 'decoy candy drawer to throw others off the trail.'
jokes.setup: Emily mentions she had a secret candy drawer at her high-powered job.
jokes.punchline: Without missing a beat, Liz identifies the need for a decoy candy drawer — revealing she has clearly thought about and possibly executed this strategy.
jokes.explanation: A gem of a joke. The concept itself (decoy candy drawer as professional strategy) is original and specific. The speed with which Liz makes the connection, and the implicit revelation that she lives this, is the joke. Excellent character integration — this is quintessentially Liz Lemon. Earns its high score.

jokes.text: Kenneth goes to Jack directly to disclose his 'relationship' with a dancer — whom he has never spoken to — citing company policy.
jokes.setup: Kenneth says he learned company policy requires disclosing workplace relationships.
jokes.punchline: He hasn't spoken to the woman — he has a 'long-term plan to marry her' and wants 'the company to be aware of his intentions.'
jokes.explanation: A fantastic Kenneth joke. His literal-minded application of rules, combined with the escalating absurdity (a non-relationship disclosed as a relationship, with long-term marriage plans for a stranger), is perfectly structured. The detail of going to Jack specifically because he doesn't trust Pete due to skull ridges is an additional layer. Only Kenneth could do this.

jokes.text: Kenneth won't go to Pete because 'he has a ridge on the section of the skull associated with deviousness.'
jokes.setup: Jack notes there are 40 people between him and Kenneth in the org chart, including Pete.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth distrusts Pete based on phrenology — skull ridge analysis.
jokes.explanation: A nice absurdist character beat — Kenneth's folk-wisdom belief in phrenology fits his wholesome, anachronistic worldview. The specificity of 'the section of the skull associated with deviousness' is very funny.

jokes.text: Kenneth: 'I actually haven't spoken to her yet, but I have a long-term plan to marry her, and I wanted the company to be aware of my intentions.'
jokes.setup: Jack asks Kenneth if he's dating one of the dancers.
jokes.punchline: He's never spoken to her but has a marriage plan — and is notifying his employer as if filing paperwork.
jokes.explanation: This is the punchline beat of the Kenneth disclosure sequence, distinct enough from the setup to score separately. The specific formality of 'wanted the company to be aware of my intentions' is the funniest line in the bit and lands harder than the setup.

jokes.text: Kenneth: 'And not because of my acute ventralitis.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth says his heart skips a beat when he watches Daphne dance.
jokes.punchline: He clarifies it's not his heart condition — 'acute ventralitis' — distinguishing romantic feelings from a medical symptom.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy — the one-line aside implies an entire backstory (Kenneth has a cardiac condition serious enough to cause heart skips, has been warned about it, and is now carefully distinguishing symptoms from emotions). The made-up condition name is plausible enough to land. Great character work.

jokes.text: Jack: 'I see. I'll be sure to mention that at the next board meeting.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth asks Jack to log that he intends to marry dancer Daphne.
jokes.punchline: Jack drily agrees to bring Kenneth's unrequited non-relationship to the Sheinhardt Universal board — a perfect straight-man deadpan.
jokes.explanation: Jack's willingness to humor Kenneth with total seriousness is a reliable comic dynamic. The line is extremely economical. Good but not exceptional — the straight-man response is a common structure, even if executed well.

jokes.text: Oh, also, I don't know if this is harassment, but someone at the Today Show made me eat an unripe banana in front of her.
jokes.setup: Kenneth is wrapping up his disclosure conversation with Jack.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth casually adds that someone (implied: Meredith Vieira) made him eat an unripe banana as a potentially harassing act — the specificity of 'unripe' makes it maximally weird.
jokes.explanation: Callbacks the Vieira joke and adds the wonderfully specific detail of an 'unripe banana' — the wrongness of the ripeness is what makes this extraordinary. The earnest 'I don't know if this is harassment' framing is pitch-perfect Kenneth. Strong 8+ justified.

jokes.text: Kenneth: 'Also, I don't know if this is harassment, but someone at the Today Show made me eat an unripe banana in front of her.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth is wrapping up his disclosure to Jack.
jokes.punchline: As an afterthought, he mentions a borderline-harassment incident involving an unripe banana — clearly describing coerced, uncomfortable behavior framed with complete innocence.
jokes.explanation: The 'unripe banana' detail is inspired — specific enough to be disturbing, weird enough to be funny, and Kenneth's framing ('I don't know if this is harassment') reveals he genuinely can't identify that he's being harassed. The escalation from throwing away his documents to forced banana-eating is perfect. One of the episode's best jokes.

jokes.text: Tracy's friend's reaction shot / non-response upon learning he'll have to disclose the relationship.
jokes.setup: The writers learn in-office relationships must be disclosed. Someone has a relationship to disclose.
jokes.punchline: A silent, wide-eyed reaction beat from one of Tracy's entourage — implying they have something to hide.
jokes.explanation: A functional reaction beat that plants the Dotcom/Daphne situation. Inferred from transcript context. Competent scene-setting but not a strong joke on its own.

jokes.text: Liz arrives at a wealthy friend's apartment in casual clothes, and the friend is 'dressed up' — for a weekday, at home. Liz: 'So this is normal? This is like your version of sweatpants and pop-tarts?' Friend: 'Not too shabs.' Liz: 'Short for shabby. Hilarious.'
jokes.setup: Liz arrives at a glamorous friend's apartment expecting her to be dressed down.
jokes.punchline: The friend uses 'shabs' (short for shabby) unironically as a positive descriptor; Liz immediately dissects the linguistic absurdity.
jokes.explanation: Liz's deadpan annotation of rich-person vocabulary is good character work. 'Short for shabby. Hilarious.' lands as a dry, self-aware line. Solid but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Jack's ways to achieve a life of leisure: 'Just short the housing market. Or write a cookbook specifically for mixed-race children. Or marry a rich, old dude who dies. Or have mild lupus and great insurance.'
jokes.setup: Jack is telling Liz she could live like his wealthy friend if she wanted.
jokes.punchline: His list of wealth strategies is increasingly dark and specific — shorting housing (callous), a niche cookbook (absurd), marrying for inheritance (mercenary), mild lupus with good insurance (weirdly specific and dark).
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes — a perfectly constructed list that escalates in absurdity and darkness. Each item is funnier than the last. 'Mild lupus and great insurance' is a masterpiece of specific dark comedy that only Jack Donaghy could offer as sincere advice. The structure is excellent: the list format creates comic rhythm, and the lupus line is an ideal final beat. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: This could be your life too, Liz. Just short the housing market. Or write a cookbook specifically for mixed-race children. Or marry a rich, old dude who dies. Or have mild lupus and great insurance.
jokes.setup: Emily is suggesting how Liz could live a life of leisure like Emily's friend group.
jokes.punchline: The list escalates from semi-plausible (short the housing market) through increasingly dark options — dying husband, mild lupus — each more absurd than the last.
jokes.explanation: A fantastic list joke with a great escalation curve. Each item on the list is darker and more specific, with 'mild lupus and great insurance' being a brilliant final beat — it's not even dramatically unlucky, just mildly unfortunate and well-insured. The specificity of 'mild' makes it. Excellent quotability.

jokes.text: Liz spends the entire speech about why she can't/shouldn't join the spa day... and then we cut to her fully participating — massages, Bergdorf, dermatologist tune-up, dinner.
jokes.setup: Liz delivers a long, earnest speech about why she really shouldn't come, she's in work mode, she won't enjoy it, etc.
jokes.punchline: She goes to everything. The audience sees her at each luxury stop mid-speech via cutaway or implied ellipsis.
jokes.explanation: A well-executed structural joke — Liz's protests are undercut by her actions in real time. The '30 Rock' rapid-cut approach makes this land harder than it would in a slower show. Good character integration; this is Liz's specific weakness (denial while indulging).

jokes.text: 'Those look great on you.' / 'Then I'm buying them.' — mid-self-pitying monologue, Liz is clearly shopping.
jokes.setup: Liz continues her monologue about needing work and thriving under stress.
jokes.punchline: A non sequitur interjection about clothing reveals Liz is actively shopping while delivering a speech about how she can't enjoy herself.
jokes.explanation: A perfectly timed one-two punch — the line interrupts Liz's lament so abruptly and she adopts it so instantly ('Then I'm buying them') that it's a great comedic beat. Very economical. The contrast with her words is the whole joke.

jokes.text: Liz: 'What time is it?' Friend: 'Almost midnight.' — Liz had promised one drink, it's now nearly midnight.
jokes.setup: Liz promised to have 'one drink' and then go home early.
jokes.punchline: It's nearly midnight — she stayed for the whole night without noticing.
jokes.explanation: A clean payoff to the running bit about Liz's inability to stop herself from enjoying the spa day. The 'almost midnight' line is delivered simply and lands well. Conventional structure but effective.

jokes.text: Liz gets home after midnight and realizes: 'I forgot to watch my show.'
jokes.setup: Liz spent the whole episode worried about missing her show.
jokes.punchline: She forgot to watch it — the thing she was obsessively stressed about, she didn't even bother to watch when she had the chance.
jokes.explanation: A great button on the spa day sequence. The irony is sharp and character-perfect — Liz's stated obsession with work dissolved the moment she had a good time, revealing her workaholism is partly anxious habit, not genuine passion for the show itself. Excellent economy — one line does enormous thematic work.

jokes.text: Jenna: 'I'm prepared to do a nipple slip if you need it.'
jokes.setup: Jenna is about to do press for the movie at the Kids' Choice Awards.
jokes.punchline: Her first instinct is to offer a nipple slip — at a children's award show.
jokes.explanation: The joke lands on the juxtaposition between the children's event and Jenna's instinctive PR toolbox. Her casualness about it ('if you need it') is perfect character work. The joke is concise and punchy.

jokes.text: Reporter asks Jenna: 'Whose mom are you?' Jenna replies: 'Thank you.'
jokes.setup: Jenna arrives at the Kids' Choice Awards expecting to be recognized.
jokes.punchline: A reporter asks if she's someone's mom (not a celebrity). Jenna responds 'Thank you' — possibly interpreting 'mom' as a compliment about her appearance, or being so out of touch she misses the insult entirely.
jokes.explanation: Two words ('Thank you.') do exceptional work here. The ambiguity of whether Jenna thinks being called someone's mom is a compliment, or whether she's so narcissistically disconnected that she misses the slight entirely, is funnier than any explicit response. Perfect economy and character integration.

jokes.text: Jenna is upstaged mid-sentence by a child shouting 'Dora the Explorer's backpack!' at the Kids' Choice Awards.
jokes.setup: Jenna is attempting to do press for her movie at the Kids' Choice Awards.
jokes.punchline: A child completely ignores her and runs toward Dora the Explorer's backpack prop — Jenna, who fought for this platform, is less interesting to children than a cartoon backpack.
jokes.explanation: A very funny visual/situational gag — Jenna's irrelevance to the target demographic is demonstrated perfectly by losing to an inanimate cartoon accessory. The specificity of 'Dora the Explorer's backpack' (not even Dora herself) makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Dotcom refuses to get Grizz extra mustard as part of their fight; Kenneth mediates: 'He'll never get mustard. Except for the mustard that comes with the sandwich.'
jokes.setup: Dotcom and Grizz are fighting and Kenneth is trying to mediate.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth undercuts his own dramatic pronouncement ('He'll never get mustard!') by immediately noting there IS mustard in the sandwich — rendering his stand meaningless.
jokes.explanation: A neat structural joke: the dramatic declaration collapses immediately under its own logic, and Kenneth doesn't notice. The deflation is very funny and his obliviousness makes it character-specific.

jokes.text: Dotcom: 'I didn't say—' Kenneth: 'I knew this would happen someday. A woman would come between us.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth mishears or overinterprets Dotcom's words as a declaration of love.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth launches into a dramatic speech about a woman coming between them — while Dotcom literally did not say what Kenneth thinks he said.
jokes.explanation: A funny misreading beat — Kenneth's romantic interpretation of a non-statement is very in-character. His 'I knew this would happen someday' melodrama is good. Solid but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Tracy: 'Liz Lemon's in jail now. And somebody has to step up and take charge around here.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth tries to stop Tracy from starting 'adventures' per Liz's instructions.
jokes.punchline: Tracy casually announces that Liz is 'in jail now' — a completely fabricated justification to do whatever he wants.
jokes.explanation: A great Tracy line — the escalation from 'suspension' to 'jail' is instant and completely committed. His self-appointment as leader ('somebody has to step up') while obviously using it as license for chaos is pure Tracy.

jokes.text: 'Let the problem solving begin.' — Tracy declares this ominously before doing something clearly problematic.
jokes.setup: Tracy has decided to take charge in Liz's absence.
jokes.punchline: 'Let the problem solving begin' as a grandiose declaration from someone who will obviously create more problems.
jokes.explanation: A well-timed button line on Tracy's self-delusion. The dramatic delivery of a mundane phrase is a reliable Tracy device. Functional and character-consistent.

jokes.text: Jenna: 'First a backpack upstages me, then the paparazzi kept calling me Dina Lohan, and now the Cyrus family has decided to rock a bunch of funky hats.'
jokes.setup: Jenna is having a disastrous night at the Kids' Choice Awards.
jokes.punchline: A rapid-fire list of indignities, including being mistaken for Lindsay Lohan's mother and being upstaged by the Cyrus family's hat choices.
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed escalation joke. 'Dina Lohan' is a precise celebrity insult (implying Jenna looks like the mother of a troubled star), and the Cyrus family hat complaint is wonderfully petty and specific. Good list structure with an absurd kicker.

jokes.text: 'Did Jackie Jormp-Jomp give up when those vampires attacked Woodstocks?'
jokes.setup: Jenna wants to give up after her bad night at the Kids' Choice Awards.
jokes.punchline: The motivational speech invokes Jackie Jormp-Jomp's fictional lore — which now includes 'vampires attacking Woodstocks,' a completely invented, escalated absurdity.
jokes.explanation: A callback that substantially raises the stakes on an already great joke. 'Vampires attacked Woodstocks' adds a layer of absurdist mythology to Jackie Jormp-Jomp that is delightful. The callback structure earns its bonus — the original joke was already strong, and this makes it better. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: The Kids' Choice Awards memorial segment for 'those we lost in the kid entertainment industry' — and Jenna's face appears.
jokes.setup: There's a touching memorial moment at the Kids' Choice Awards for deceased entertainers.
jokes.punchline: Jenna is in the memorial reel — she is not dead, but she's apparently so irrelevant that the producers think she is.
jokes.explanation: A brilliantly dark plot point played as comedy — the memorial reel gag is funny both as a situation (she's alive) and as a character indignity (she's so forgotten they thought she died). Sets up the entire Tupac subplot.

jokes.text: From DreamWorks's upcoming feature film 'On Top of Spaghetti,' Helen Mirren.
jokes.setup: A presenter at the Kids' Choice Awards is being introduced.
jokes.punchline: Helen Mirren is presenting at a children's awards show, and the film she's promoting is called 'On Top of Spaghetti' — a DreamWorks project named after the children's song.
jokes.explanation: The joke is the incongruity of Helen Mirren at a kids' show, and the movie title being a nursery rhyme. Quick and funny as a background gag.

jokes.text: Was that me? Did they just say I'm dead? / I thought you spoke to the producers.
jokes.setup: Jenna has just seen herself eulogized at the Kids' Choice Awards.
jokes.punchline: Her handler's response — 'I thought you spoke to the producers' — implies the responsibility has been fully passed around and nobody actually stopped it.
jokes.explanation: Functional joke — the 'thought you handled it' chaos is relatable, but doesn't have a particularly strong punchline.

jokes.text: Jack: 'I want to Tupac you.' Jenna: 'Fine. But I have to pee first.' Jack: 'No, no, no — Tupac Shakur, the rapper.'
jokes.setup: Jack is pitching a marketing strategy using the accidental death announcement.
jokes.punchline: Jenna interprets 'I want to Tupac you' as a sex act. Jack has to clarify it's a marketing reference.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's top jokes. The double entendre is set up perfectly — Jenna's sexual interpretation is completely in character and her pragmatic 'Fine. But I have to pee first.' is a spectacular punchline before the real punchline. The clarification ('No, no, no — Tupac Shakur, the rapper') is the button that confirms what we suspected. Extremely quotable. High impact.

jokes.text: Jenna on the Tupac marketing strategy: 'Die young, become a legend. Just like Janis. Or Rusty, the bear from the Magicals.'
jokes.setup: Jack explains that dead artists sell more — like Tupac, like Janis Joplin.
jokes.punchline: Jenna adds 'Rusty, the bear from the Magicals' to the list of legendary dead — a completely fictional, obscure reference that deflates the mythologizing.
jokes.explanation: The fake reference — 'Rusty, the bear from the Magicals' — is a 30 Rock specialty: a made-up cultural touchstone that sounds just plausible enough to make you wonder. The joke is in the contrast between real legends and this invented obscurity. Jenna's genuine belief in Rusty's legendary status is perfect.

jokes.text: Jenna: 'Oh, I can play dead. I watched my whole church group get eaten by a bear.'
jokes.setup: Jack tells Jenna she just needs to stay dead (pretend to be dead for publicity).
jokes.punchline: Jenna agrees she can play dead — because she learned from watching her church group get eaten by a bear.
jokes.explanation: The episode's single best joke. The sheer darkness of the reveal (Jenna's church group was eaten by a bear), delivered with complete casualness as a skill-building life experience, is extraordinary. It expands Jenna's mythology in a single line, is completely unexpected, wildly specific, and has the economy of a perfectly constructed joke. The callback to 'Rusty the bear' seconds earlier makes it even richer on rewatch. Genuinely exceptional — closest to the 9.5-anchor in this episode.

jokes.text: Congratulations, Miss Lemon. You've completed your sensitivity training. Your suspension is up, and here is your certificate.
jokes.setup: Liz has been attending sexual harassment seminars throughout the episode.
jokes.punchline: The callback to the opening seminar, now concluding — the formality of a 'certificate' for not harassing people is mildly funny.
jokes.explanation: Functional closure to the seminar subplot. Not particularly funny on its own — the certificate joke is predictable and the setup doesn't have a strong payoff here.

jokes.text: The sensitivity training facilitator celebrates Liz's completion but says 'coming back to work isn't always easy' and launches into a vivid description of workplace misery.
jokes.setup: The facilitator is supposed to be encouraging Liz to return to work.
jokes.punchline: His 'encouragement' is a relentlessly bleak description of work — pointless meetings, futility, creeping closer to the grave — which functions as an accidental anti-work manifesto.
jokes.explanation: An ironic reversal — the rehabilitation counselor inadvertently summarizes the nightmare of modern work with deadpan accuracy. The 'creep closer and closer to the grave' is a strong line. Solid sustained bit.

jokes.text: That's soon.
jokes.setup: The instructor tells Liz she can return to work tomorrow.
jokes.punchline: Liz, who has been ostensibly desperate to return to work, reacts with 'That's soon' — betraying her newfound ambivalence about going back.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully economical character beat. Two words ('That's soon') convey Liz's entire arc in this episode — she's been seduced by leisure and is now dreading return. The reversal from her earlier desperation is the joke.

jokes.text: That's soon.
jokes.setup: Liz is told her suspension is up and she can go back to work tomorrow.
jokes.punchline: After days of claiming she desperately misses work, her immediate response to returning is 'That's soon.'
jokes.explanation: Two words — 'That's soon' — completely subvert the entire A-plot of the episode. Liz has been presented as desperate to return to work, and the instant it's available, she hedges. The economy is perfect (10/10), the character reversal is earned and honest, and it recontextualizes everything. Among the episode's top jokes.

jokes.text: Liz to the facilitator: 'Why don't you drop those Dockers and gimme a piece of that sweet ass?'
jokes.setup: The facilitator asks if there are any questions after his inadvertently depressing pep talk.
jokes.punchline: Liz — at her own reinstatement sensitivity training — sexually harasses the facilitator.
jokes.explanation: A spectacular structural callback — the entire episode's sexual harassment seminar thread pays off with Liz, who was never supposed to have harassed anyone, actually committing harassment in the most ironic possible context: the reinstatement hearing for her sensitivity training. The specific line ('drop those Dockers... sweet ass') is unexpectedly coarse and very funny. The callback earns its high score completely. One of the episode's top moments.

jokes.text: Jack on phone: 'Jeffrey Weener-slave said you put your fingers in his mouth. Did I? Or did he put his mouth on my fingers?'
jokes.setup: Jack is confronting Liz about extending her suspension by harassing the facilitator.
jokes.punchline: Liz's defense is a semantic reversal — she didn't put her fingers in his mouth; he put his mouth on her fingers. The distinction is meaningless but she believes it.
jokes.explanation: A great joke with a hidden callback — Liz uses the exact same non-defense that Jenna used earlier (it was the victim's fault for making contact). The parallel is elegant. The line itself is highly quotable and lands hard. Excellent economy and character integration.

jokes.text: Jack: 'It's gonna take at least six weeks paid leave to get to the bottom of this.'
jokes.setup: Jack is supposedly upset about Liz extending her suspension.
jokes.punchline: His 'outrage' immediately converts to an outcome that benefits Liz (more paid leave) — suggesting he may be gaming the system too.
jokes.explanation: A decent beat — Jack's loyalty to Liz manifesting as bureaucratic manipulation. The 'six weeks paid leave' as resolution to a harassment complaint is a nice dark joke about corporate HR. Solid.

jokes.text: Jack: 'I'm very busy right now faking Jenna's death to sell her movie.' Liz: 'I'm not going to engage on that. Mantra.'
jokes.setup: Jack calls Liz in the middle of his Jenna scheme.
jokes.punchline: Jack casually mentions he's 'faking Jenna's death' as if it's a normal work task; Liz refuses to engage and retreats to a mantra.
jokes.explanation: The casualness of 'faking Jenna's death' as a work item — and Liz's 'I'm not going to engage on that. Mantra.' as a coping mechanism — is excellent. The idea that she needs a mantra to resist engaging with 30 Rock absurdity is a great meta-character moment.

jokes.text: Liz says she's on 'humanity leave.' Jack: 'Good god, what Indigo Girls song is that from?'
jokes.setup: Liz invents a new type of leave — 'humanity leave' — to describe her lifestyle experiment.
jokes.punchline: Jack immediately identifies it as sounding like an Indigo Girls song title, mocking the earnestness of the phrase.
jokes.explanation: An extremely efficient joke. 'Humanity leave' is a funny concept, but Jack's snap identification of it as an Indigo Girls song title is the real joke — a precise cultural shorthand for earnest, liberal folksiness that feels both accurate and specific. Very quotable and very Jack.

jokes.text: Liz: 'Syllabus of Us: Off-Vagabonds, Martyrs, and Quilts.'
jokes.setup: Jack asks what Indigo Girls song 'humanity leave' is from.
jokes.punchline: Liz immediately invents a completely convincing fake Indigo Girls song/album title that sounds exactly like what they would name something.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's finest jokes. The fake song title 'Syllabus of Us: Off-Vagabonds, Martyrs, and Quilts' is a comedic masterwork — it perfectly captures the aesthetic of earnest, political folk music with the specific details (vagabonds, martyrs, quilts) that feel hilariously accurate. The use of 'quilts' as the final item in the list is the ideal absurdist kicker. Extremely quotable. One of the best jokes in the episode.

jokes.text: Jack: 'Lemon, you are not a rich divorcee.' Liz: 'I know. But I have some money saved — enough for two years. Maybe four if I give up cable. So I will be back to the show in four years.'
jokes.setup: Jack tells Liz she's fooling herself trying to live like his wealthy friend Emily.
jokes.punchline: Liz does the math — four years if she gives up cable — and announces she'll be back in four years, treating this as a reasonable work plan.
jokes.explanation: A great Liz character moment — her idea of 'living richly' is just slightly extending her runway by cutting cable. The immediate 'back to the show in four years' treats her sabbatical like a scheduled return. Very character-specific.

jokes.text: How do you know all these Indigo Girls songs?
jokes.setup: Jack quotes what sounds like an Indigo Girls lyric back at Liz.
jokes.punchline: Liz asks how Jack knows all the Indigo Girls songs — implying he's familiar enough to identify them, which is incongruous with his alpha-male persona.
jokes.explanation: A great callback that flips the joke back on Jack. The implication that Jack Donaghy has extensive knowledge of Indigo Girls is funny and the question is left perfectly unanswered.

jokes.text: Jack: 'There is no solace in their luxury. Only deep despair.' Liz: 'How do you know all these Indigo Girls songs?'
jokes.setup: Jack makes a dramatically gloomy observation about rich idle women.
jokes.punchline: Liz fires back that his melodramatic phrase also sounds like an Indigo Girls song — the callback lands because Jack had just criticized Liz for her 'humanity leave' phrasing.
jokes.explanation: A near-perfect callback execution. Jack's own language ('no solace... only deep despair') gets caught by the same trap he set for Liz, and her deadpan 'How do you know all these Indigo Girls songs?' implies Jack is an Indigo Girls fan — an unexpectedly humanizing and very funny revelation. Excellent economy and structure. One of the best callback moments in the episode.

jokes.text: Oh, God, there's a spider nest in my yoga mat!
jokes.setup: Jack is trying to convince Liz that Emily's lifestyle group is secretly miserable.
jokes.punchline: Perfectly timed, Emily screams about a spider nest in her yoga mat — validating Jack's claim mid-sentence.
jokes.explanation: A great structural joke — the universe immediately validates Jack's prediction. The spider nest is a wonderfully specific, disgusting detail, and the timing (mid-Jack-lecture) is ideal. Good structural comedy.

jokes.text: Tracy: 'Friendship and trust in the entourage is the most important thing. Like that HBO show. John Adams.'
jokes.setup: Tracy explains why he fired Daphne — to restore friendship and trust in his entourage.
jokes.punchline: His reference for an HBO show about friendship and trust is 'John Adams' — a historical mini-series about a founding father, not an entourage at all.
jokes.explanation: A fantastic Tracy Jordan joke. The deliberate misidentification of 'John Adams' as the HBO show about entourage friendship (when the obvious reference would be 'Entourage') is brilliantly specific. It implies Tracy has seen 'John Adams' and interpreted it as a buddy show — which is more absurd and funnier. Very high character integration and economy.

jokes.text: Tracy: 'Heavy is the head that eats the crayons.'
jokes.setup: Tracy has just identified that he normally relies on Liz to clean up his messes.
jokes.punchline: He misquotes 'heavy lies the head that wears the crown' — replacing 'wears the crown' with 'eats the crayons,' implying his burden of leadership involves eating crayons.
jokes.explanation: The episode's single most quotable line and the strongest pure joke. The misquotation of Shakespeare ('heavy lies the head that wears the crown' → 'heavy is the head that eats the crayons') is a perfect character encapsulation — Tracy's grandiosity, his non-sequitur worldview, and his particular brand of dumb-but-kind-of-profound absurdism are all captured in nine words. It's specific (crayons, not anything else), rhythmically perfect, and deeply Tracy. Deserves its exceptional score.

jokes.text: Pete. A word. / Jenna's dead. / I don't feel anything. / What's wrong with me?
jokes.setup: Jack pulls Pete aside to tell him about Jenna's (fake) death.
jokes.punchline: Pete's immediate reaction is 'I don't feel anything' followed by 'What's wrong with me?' — his concern is not grief but his own lack of grief.
jokes.explanation: A brilliantly economical joke. Pete's first reaction to Jenna's death is the absence of reaction, and his concern is therapeutic rather than empathetic. The four-beat exchange (word → dead → nothing → wrong with me) is perfectly structured. Very quotable.

jokes.text: They already have an obituary reel for Jenna — 'We put it together after she cheated on that mobster.'
jokes.setup: Jack says they need to put together an on-air tribute for Jenna.
jokes.punchline: They already have one pre-produced — because Jenna previously had a life-threatening situation involving a mobster she cheated on.
jokes.explanation: A great character-building dark joke. The idea that TGS has a pre-made Jenna obituary reel (for practical reasons) is already funny; the explanation — she cheated on a mobster — expands her mythology hilariously. The casual delivery makes it land harder.

jokes.text: Emily: 'Oh, eating right, working out, sleeping... Bm-ing like a rock star?'
jokes.setup: Liz lists the healthy things she's been doing during her leave.
jokes.punchline: Emily adds 'BM-ing like a rock star' to the list of health metrics — the most Liz Lemon-appropriate addition possible.
jokes.explanation: A good low-comedy moment — the specificity of 'like a rock star' applied to bowel movements is a reliable Liz-adjacent joke. Emily seems to know Liz well already, which is a quick character beat.

jokes.text: All right, all right. What's the hump day schedule look like? / Oh, it's easy, Liz, it's Thursday. / I read somewhere it's Tuesday.
jokes.setup: Liz is slipping into 'work mode' during her leisure time.
jokes.punchline: She asks about a 'hump day' schedule, Emily corrects that it's Thursday, and a third friend confidently states she read it was Tuesday — a beautifully absurd escalation of calendar ignorance.
jokes.explanation: The escalation of day-of-week confusion — each woman more wrong and more confident — is a funny joke about the temporal dissolution that comes with a life of total leisure. 'I read somewhere it's Tuesday' is the best beat.

jokes.text: Tracy has replaced the fired professional dancers with women 'who were brawling in a parking lot an hour ago' — now presented as the new TGS dancers.
jokes.setup: The TGS dancers quit in solidarity with Daphne.
jokes.punchline: Tracy's solution: hire strangers from a parking lot brawl as replacement dancers.
jokes.explanation: Very Tracy — the solution to a personnel problem is to find people mid-brawl and give them jobs. The time detail ('an hour ago') grounds the absurdity perfectly. Good character integration.

jokes.text: My boss kept trying to tell me that I would go crazy living a life of leisure, that it's unhealthy — well, he's actually right.
jokes.setup: Liz tells Emily that her boss was wrong about leisure being unhealthy.
jokes.punchline: She immediately corrects herself mid-sentence to admit he's actually right — her moment of self-awareness is immediate and abrupt.
jokes.explanation: A functional character beat — Liz's mid-sentence pivot from defending Jack to agreeing with him is a good Liz moment. Not exceptional.

jokes.text: Emily: 'I used to be a neurosurgeon before Jasmine Guy and I wrote our cookbook.'
jokes.setup: Emily is explaining that the brain needs stimulation.
jokes.punchline: She mentions she was a neurosurgeon — then casually notes she gave it up to co-write a cookbook with Jasmine Guy (a specific B-list celebrity).
jokes.explanation: A great absurdist detail — the specificity of Jasmine Guy (a recognizable but surprising celebrity choice) as cookbook co-author is very funny. The neurosurgeon-to-cookbook pipeline is a good joke about what rich women do with their lives. Very 30 Rock in its celebrity-detail specificity.

jokes.text: What, like Sudoku? / Uh, we did a games night for a couple of weeks. Didn't last. / So, charity work? / No, charity work sucks.
jokes.setup: Liz is asking what the women do to combat brain atrophy.
jokes.punchline: After dismissing Sudoku and rejecting charity work with 'No, charity work sucks,' the conversation builds to reveal the actual activity is Fight Club.
jokes.explanation: A great escalating misdirection sequence. 'Charity work sucks' as a flat rejection from wealthy leisure women is very funny, and the whole exchange builds to the Fight Club reveal. Structural excellence.

jokes.text: The 'special activity' is revealed to be a fight club — Erin punches herself in the face as a demonstration.
jokes.setup: The women build tension around revealing their 'special activity' with Liz guessing innocuous hobbies.
jokes.punchline: It's a fight club. A group of wealthy, privileged women beat each other up to feel alive.
jokes.explanation: The reveal is well-earned — the setup perfectly misdirects. Wealthy women doing fight club as a substitute for purpose is a sharp social satire. The structure (escalating guesses → abrupt dark reveal) is excellent.

jokes.text: Punch me in the face, Liz. / I'm sorry, what? / You heard me. Punch me as hard as you can, and then I am coming at you like an animal.
jokes.setup: Liz has just been told about the 'special activity' these women do to combat boredom.
jokes.punchline: Emily's 'special activity' is a Fight Club — she wants Liz to punch her in the face as hard as she can.
jokes.explanation: The Fight Club reveal is excellent. The build from mystery to absurdist conclusion (wealthy divorcees punching each other) is well-structured. 'Coming at you like an animal' from this elegant woman is a great tonal mismatch. The misdirection across multiple dialogue beats is impressive.

jokes.text: Liz: 'Oh god, is this a fight club?' Emily: 'The pain proves we're alive.' Liz: 'Oh, this is very disappointing!'
jokes.setup: The fight club is revealed.
jokes.punchline: Liz's reaction to discovering a fight club is not fear or excitement but genuine disappointment — as if she expected something better.
jokes.explanation: 'Oh, this is very disappointing!' is a perfect Liz Lemon line — her reaction to a fight club is not adrenaline but letdown, which is deeply character-specific. The contrast between the dramatic reveal and Liz's mild, professorial disappointment is very funny.

jokes.text: Liz: 'I brought a roll of quarters to hold in my fist.' — before reluctantly agreeing to fight.
jokes.setup: The women are urging Liz to punch someone to join the fight club.
jokes.punchline: Liz reveals she came prepared with brass-knuckle quarters — implying she was considering this possibility, or is always prepared for street fighting.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best Liz Lemon jokes. The detail that she has a roll of quarters on her person — for use in a fist fight — is wildly specific and implies either preparation or a permanent state of low-grade urban paranoia. It's deeply Liz. Very quotable and high economy.

jokes.text: Oh god. Jack was right. / Oh, I have to get back to my show. I need the show.
jokes.setup: Liz realizes she's been pulled into Fight Club.
jokes.punchline: Her epiphany isn't 'I should get out of here' but 'Jack was right' — her immediate reference point is Jack's earlier wisdom, and she needs her show as much as it needs her.
jokes.explanation: Clean A-plot resolution moment. 'Jack was right' as a revelation is both character-true and slightly ironic given Liz's resistance to his advice throughout.

jokes.text: Liz: 'Oh god. Jack was right.' (about her needing to go back to work) — delivered in the context of a fight club.
jokes.setup: Liz has just been asked to join a women's fight club.
jokes.punchline: The lesson she takes from the fight club is not about fight clubs but that Jack was right — this life of leisure has driven her to extremes.
jokes.explanation: A satisfying thematic callback — Jack's prediction is confirmed in the most extreme possible way. The economy of 'Jack was right' doing all the work is good. Functional rather than exceptional.

jokes.text: Emily: 'You want out, Liz? You're gonna have to fight your way out.'
jokes.setup: Liz says she needs to get back to work.
jokes.punchline: Emily tells Liz she must fight her way out of the fight club — as if it's a gang.
jokes.explanation: A solid button on the fight club sequence. The commitment to fight club rules by wealthy women is funny, and the line works as an absurdist escalation of the premise. Efficient.

jokes.text: A memorial tribute for Jenna on TGS begins with: 'The coast guard won't officially declare her dead yet, but what the pirates did to that boat!'
jokes.setup: TGS is running a tribute for the 'deceased' Jenna Maroney.
jokes.punchline: The tribute references pirates having done something horrible to a boat — escalating Jenna's fake death to a maritime pirate attack.
jokes.explanation: A superb escalation of the fake death scheme — 'what the pirates did to that boat!' implies a story too awful to specify, and the coast guard detail makes it feel real. The specificity of maritime piracy as Jenna's cause of death is perfect 30 Rock absurdism. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Jenna's tribute reel: 'That was some of Jenna Maroney's earlier work. It's hard to believe that both of those women outlived her. Especially the woman on the right.'
jokes.setup: A clip plays in Jenna's tribute.
jokes.punchline: The announcer notes both women in the clip outlived Jenna, then adds 'especially the woman on the right' — implying someone particularly sickly or elderly outlived the supposedly young Jenna.
jokes.explanation: A mean-spirited and very funny additional jab in the tribute — 'especially the woman on the right' implies visual context that reads as an insult to Jenna's apparent health/age. Dark and specific.

jokes.text: Jenna, watching her own tribute: 'It has the year I was born on it. The real year. Not the actress year.'
jokes.setup: Jenna and Jack watch her tribute on TGS and Jenna has a problem with it.
jokes.punchline: The problem is not that she's being declared dead — it's that the memorial graphic shows her actual birth year rather than the younger age she presents professionally.
jokes.explanation: An exceptional character joke. The distinction between 'the real year' and 'the actress year' is inspired — it implies Jenna has an official false age she maintains professionally, and her complaint about the memorial is entirely about vanity rather than being declared dead. 'The actress year' is a fantastic coinage. Highly quotable and deeply Jenna.

jokes.text: Jack: 'It's too late to change it, Jack.' — Jenna says this, not Jack.
jokes.setup: Jenna is panicking about her birth year being displayed.
jokes.punchline: In her panic, Jenna addresses Jack as 'Jack' while she herself is the one saying 'It's too late to change it' — she's essentially talking to herself through Jack's voice, or has become confused about who is who.
jokes.explanation: A possible transcript oddity or a quick Jenna character beat — her confusion in a crisis moment. If intentional, it's a mild character beat. Not a strong joke in isolation — may be a subtitle attribution error.

jokes.text: Ladies and gentlemen, Itzhak Bemelmans and the Tracy Jordan Dancers.
jokes.setup: The tribute to Jenna is supposed to culminate in a musical performance.
jokes.punchline: The performer is 'Itzhak Bemelmans' — a hybrid of Itzhak Perlman (famous violinist) and Ludwig Bemelmans (Madeline author) — apparently performing with Tracy's parking lot brawler dancers.
jokes.explanation: A quick absurdist background joke — the fake musician name and the convergence of the episode's storylines (the dancers meeting the Jenna tribute) is neatly constructed.

jokes.text: Jenna: 'Still alive. Not yet 32. Sorry, Jack. Worth it.'
jokes.setup: Jenna has blown up the entire fake death scheme by grabbing a microphone and performing live, proving she's alive — and announcing her age.
jokes.punchline: 'Not yet 32' — Jenna's vanity (correcting the birth year) is the reason she destroyed a million-dollar marketing scheme. 'Worth it.' is the kicker.
jokes.explanation: A spectacular payoff to the Jenna death scheme. The entire subplot collapses because Jenna couldn't bear the wrong birth year being public. 'Worth it.' is the perfect button — she has zero regrets. 'Not yet 32' is a precise, character-perfect line. The economy is extraordinary — four short sentences carry the weight of the entire subplot's resolution. One of the episode's finest jokes.

jokes.text: Liz returns: 'I'm back.' Jack: 'What did it turn out to be? Lesbians?' Liz: 'No. Fight club.'
jokes.setup: Jack predicted Liz would come back (he said the leisure life was unlivable); he now asks what broke her.
jokes.punchline: Jack's first guess is 'Lesbians?' — a non sequitur that implies he had a specific theory. The actual answer ('Fight club') is equally absurd.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best exchanges. The three-beat structure (Liz returns → Jack guesses 'Lesbians?' → 'No. Fight club.') is extraordinarily economical. Jack's guess implies he's seen this pattern before and has a standard list of answers, and 'Lesbians?' is a perfect absurdist first entry. 'Fight club' as a straight answer tops it. The whole sequence in four words after 'I'm back.' Exceptional economy and structure.

jokes.text: Liz, back at TGS, sees the chaos and launches into a rant: 'You guys mess up everything you touch, and then I have to come in here and fix it.' — then immediately starts smiling and hugging them.
jokes.setup: Liz returns to TGS to find it in chaos — dancers from a parking lot brawl performing, everything a mess.
jokes.punchline: Her angry rant gives way to pure happiness — she's smiling, then hugging Tracy and others. She needed this. The chaos IS her medicine.
jokes.explanation: A satisfying thematic and comedic payoff. The transition from rage to joy is the joke — Liz's identity is so fused with her chaotic workplace that even the fury of returning is pleasurable. Tracy's observation 'Why are you smiling? You're freaking me out.' is a good additional beat. Strong character work.

jokes.text: Tracy: 'Why are you smiling? You're freaking me out.'
jokes.setup: Liz is ranting at them while visibly smiling.
jokes.punchline: Tracy points out the incongruity — Liz is expressing anger while clearly happy, and it disturbs him.
jokes.explanation: A quick, sharp reaction beat. Tracy noticing Liz's inappropriate smile and being genuinely unsettled is funny and character-consistent (Tracy is actually perceptive in weird ways). Good economy.

jokes.text: Why are you smiling? / You're freaking me out.
jokes.setup: Liz is yelling at Tracy and Kenneth about the chaos they've caused.
jokes.punchline: They notice she's smiling while telling them off — she's happy to be back, no matter how angry she claims to be.
jokes.explanation: A good reaction beat — Tracy and Kenneth noticing what the audience sees is a solid joke structure. The 'You're freaking me out' is a nice secondary beat.

jokes.text: Final tag: 'I'm back, nerds.'
jokes.setup: Liz has reunited with her chaotic work family.
jokes.punchline: 'I'm back, nerds.' — a triumphant, affectionate sign-off that encapsulates Liz's relationship with her workplace.
jokes.explanation: A near-perfect episode button. Three words close the entire storyline with warmth, self-awareness, and just the right level of affection-disguised-as-insult. The economy is flawless. 'Nerds' is the exactly right word. It's a callback, a character statement, and a punchline simultaneously.

tmdb_overview: During her short-term suspension, Liz is lost without TGS and the stress that comes with her job. Jack works with Jenna so she can use her celebrity status to generate some promotional buzz for her Janis Joplin bio-film.
insight: Jackie Jormp Jomp lands 75 jokes in 22 minutes—Liz's absurdist chaos peaks at 3.3-per-minute density.
